answers.1: The Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC) is deciding how much of the money that larger businesses pay on "real-time" prices (hourly prices, as far as I can tell) gets counted toward fuel costs. The more that gets counted, the lower everyone else's fuel charge is supposed to be. Side questions are mixed in: who pays certain pipeline fees, and whether solar and wind "take-or-pay" contracts and costs like coal rail car leases get counted. The PSC's five commissioners decide: Jason Shaw (chairman), Lauren "Bubba" McDonald (vice chairman), Peter Hubbard, Alicia M. Johnson and Stan Wise. The vote is scheduled for Dec 15, 2026, 9:30 a.m., at a public session in hearing room 110, 244 Washington St., Atlanta. A committee of the commissioners (the Energy Committee) takes it up first on Dec 10.
answers.2: Probably both, on different parts of the bill, and the page can't say which wins. It says that if the PSC adopts any proposed plan, my fuel charge would likely drop, but base rates could later rise to recover the same money, and whether I come out ahead depends on Georgia Power's next base rate case. There's no dollar amount. The decision is set for Dec 15, 2026 and the case must be finished by Dec 31, 2026, but the page doesn't say when a change would show up on my bill or when that next base rate case is. Why it can't say: no filing it read gives a typical home's net; Georgia Power's estimates are blacked out and the public copy doesn't say why; only PIA Staff's plan has public estimates (it doesn't say of what), and I didn't see those numbers on these screens. The "Not known yet" and "Decided now, and decided later" headings on the Summary tab showed nothing until tapped. It also doesn't say what happens to my bill if the PSC keeps today's method. GAM, the manufacturers' group, says medium and large businesses would gain more than small businesses and homes.
answers.3: The money is what larger businesses on real-time prices pay Georgia Power. Today some of it is counted toward fuel costs, which lowers the fuel charge for customers on standard rates, including homes like mine. Every proposed plan would count more of it toward fuel, so my fuel charge would likely go down. But GAM says that money now lowers other customers' base costs, so moving more of it to fuel could push base rates up later. The page says base rates could rise "to recover the same money," so it sounds like this is mostly about which part of the bill, and which customers, carry the costs; it doesn't say whether Georgia Power itself ends up with more or less. This case isn't about the businesses' hourly prices, only how their payments are split between fuel and base costs. Pipeline fees are a second money question: today standard-rate fuel charges pay them; Georgia Power and GIPL want new pipeline fees tied to large-load customers charged to those customers, and PIA Staff wants all pipeline and storage fees shared by all customers by energy use. The page never gives a total dollar amount. The "Where the money comes from" heading and each plan's "who benefits / who pays" details only open with a tap, so I couldn't see them.
answers.4: 1) Send a comment to the PSC before the vote. Comments are due 24 hours before the Dec 15 vote, which the page works out as 9:30 a.m. on Dec 14, 2026 (the earliest possible cutoff; it moves if the vote moves). The page doesn't say how to send one, so I'd have to ask: call 404-656-4501 (local) or 1-800-282-5813 (outside metro-Atlanta) and press 2, or email gapsc@psc.state.ga.us. 2) Maybe speak at the Nov 12, 2026 hearing (listed at 9:35 a.m.; arrive about 9:05 a.m. to sign in), but the page says no filing it read says whether the public will be heard that day, so call first. I didn't see where the Nov 12 hearing is held. If I go, I can ask to have written comments entered into the record. 3) Watch the Dec 15 vote, 9:30 a.m., in hearing room 110, 244 Washington St., Atlanta; it's open to the public. The Dec 10 committee meeting is in the PSC hearing room, but the page couldn't find whether the public may attend. 4) Read the case filings on the PSC's page for Docket 57171. For disability help, call (404) 656-4501; an earlier notice asked for at least one day's notice. The page doesn't say how much a comment counts; it says commissioners decide based on the evidence presented at the hearings.
answers.5: The page defines them. "Mixed" means the sources give conflicting accounts, so they disagree. "Uncertain" means nothing they found settles it yet. On the cards they're tied to one point, like "Supported; Mixed on whom the contracts serve" or, on GAM's card, "Supported; Uncertain on how base rates would move." The page calls them evidence labels, so they rate the evidence, not the plans. The exact rule is behind a "This page's exact rule" tap I couldn't see. On cards marked both "Supported" and "Mixed," the page doesn't say which claim is the supported one. Some notes were too short to follow, like "Mixed on two main points" (which points?) and "Mixed on base-side share, peak prices."
answers.6: For a change: PIA Staff and GIPL (the interfaith group) say leaving fuel-related costs like coal rail car leases out of the credit makes customers who pay the fuel charge, like me, absorb those costs. GIPL's witness John D. Wilson says today's credit "shifts costs to FCR customers." Against: GAM, the manufacturers' group, through its witness Jonathan Ly, says "increasing the RTP fuel credit would put upward pressure on base rates," and GAM says real-time money already lowers other customers' base costs.

seemed_to_favor: Mostly even. It quotes each group in its own words, says it doesn't recommend an option, and keeps repeating that base rates could rise later, which is the manufacturers' main point. Still, a few things nudged me toward the "count more toward fuel" side: six of the nine argument cards argue for a change and three argue for keeping things as they are or limiting the shift (the page says the voices reflect who filed testimony, not how many people hold each view); every card opens with what happens to the fuel charge, so the change cards lead with a plain benefit to me ("would likely lower fuel charges"), while GAM's base-rate point is put as "GAM says" and marked "Uncertain"; the headline talks only about lowering others' fuel charges; and the background quotes Georgia Power saying the review was sought "to ensure such customers pay their share of costs" and GIPL saying the method raised other customers' fuel costs, with no reply from the manufacturers there. Smaller things: GIPL is "a group of congregations" while GAM's members are described as big power users, which made one sound selfless and the other self-interested (though the page says it found nothing on GIPL members' power use), and Georgia Power's estimates being "blacked out" made the utility sound secretive.
hardest: Question 3 (whose money moves and where). The page explains it with "fuel side" vs. "base side," "the credit," take-or-pay contracts and pipeline-fee splits, but never says in plain words what the fuel charge and base rates are on my bill or gives dollar amounts, and the "Where the money comes from" section stays closed until tapped, so I pieced it together from three tabs and still wasn't sure.
